chunks: "Saturation is when the inductor's magnetic core can't carry any more flux.
A core works by having high permeability: the magnetic domains in the material line up with the field and multiply the flux, which is why you get lots of inductance from a few turns.
Once the flux density reaches the material's saturation level, basically all the domains are already aligned, and extra current adds flux only as if the core were air.
So the inductance collapses. A 10 microhenries inductor might drop to 2 or 3 microhenries or even lower.
And since di over dt equals V over L , the same voltage now ramps the current much faster.
On a scope, you see the inductor current ramp in a buck converter suddenly bend upward into a sharp spike at the end of the on-time.

That causes real problems: the switch sees a big current spike, you can trip the current limit or destroy the MOSFET, losses and heating go up, and since a hotter ferrite saturates at lower current it can run away thermally.
So when I pick an inductor I check its saturation current against the peak current, which is the DC load plus half the ripple, plus margin for transients and temperature.
Ferrite saturates hard and abruptly, while powdered-iron cores saturate softly, losing inductance gradually."
